You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Global declines in coastal habitats and wildlife have devastating consequences for Indigenous Peoples. In some places, hydropower development has environmental impacts that contribute significantly to coastal habitat loss. As development is rejuvenated for the carbon-neutral transition, mitigation of further coastal habitat impacts depends on assessing the relative and interactive effects of climate change and hydropower development. Here, we follow a detection and attribution framework to understand the collapse and limited recovery of a social-ecological system including eelgrass (Zostera marina, shikaapaashkw), geese (Branta spp., niskandiyiwaapuwaau), and Cree (Eeyou) in subarctic eastern James Bay, Canada (Eeyou Istchee). Informed by historical observations, Indigenous knowledge, and scientific research, we attribute the collapse of eelgrass and shifts in the associated social-ecological system to ecological effects of hydroelectric development (1978-1996), which degraded local environments causing eelgrass declines. Climate-driven extreme events (1998 onward) compounded losses and ecological feedbacks extended eelgrass declines all along the coast. Eelgrass recovery today appears limited by poor water clarity, altered sediments, hydrologic changes from development, and a new climate regime. Eeyou have adapted by shifting their relationships with the coastal habitat. Comprehensive assessments for hydropower developments should explicitly consider coastal social-ecological dynamics and the possible compounding impacts of climate change.

---

## Introduction

Coastal habitats have supported human communities for hundreds of thousands of years. Coastlines provide food, shelter, and access to marine and freshwater environments that define the culture, livelihoods, and identities of Indigenous Peoples who have lived along marine shorelines for countless generations1. The destruction and loss of coastal habitats worldwide during the past century2 thus has gravely affected both social systems and ecosystems3. Coastal habitat protection, management and restoration can contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation4,5, biodiversity conservation6, and Indigenous self-determination. However, the interaction of local and global environmental change to cause habitat loss and prevent habitat recovery4 is a critical knowledge gap compromising current coastal restoration efforts and preventing true cost accounting of various development activities.

Seagrasses are foundation species in many coastal ecosystems. They provide critical habitat for marine and semi-aquatic wildlife, such as waterfowl, and the reliable, nearshore wildlife harvesting opportunities in seagrass ecosystems have been particularly important for many coastal Indigenous Peoples’ food security and cultural continuity (cf. 5–9). Recently, seagrass ecosystems have also gained attention because of their tendency to accumulate carbon (“blue carbon”), in addition to being biodiversity hotspots. Protecting and restoring degraded seagrass ecosystems may thus contribute to numerous benefits for both Indigenous and non-Indigenous coastal communities, as well as for the ecosystems themselves10–12.

Many seagrass populations around the globe have massively declined in the past century. Few have fully recovered to their historical depth and spatial extents, although North Atlantic eelgrass lost to widespread wasting disease in the 1930s is considered naturally recovered in many areas, and recovered as a result of active restoration in other areas13,14. Incomplete recovery of degraded seagrass ecosystems is often characterized by lower shoot density15, reduced depth extent16, and/or reduced spatial extent16–18 of meadows relative to historical observations, as well as reduced usage by wildlife and ecological functions such as carbon storage19. The reasons for failure to fully recover can be unclear, especially when proximate causes of declines and related environmental conditions have improved18–21.

Among the potential ultimate causes of ecological changes in seagrass ecosystems are local and regional land use and development activities in watersheds that alter riverine fluxes of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment, and cause localized deterioration of water quality and poor water column light conditions due to elevated concentrations of suspended sediments13,14. Sedimentation is a well-recognized stressor because it can disrupt the natural feedback loops that keep seagrass meadows healthy: i.e., excess sediment makes water more turbid, reducing light availability and consequently slowing seagrass growth22,23. Dams are well-know drivers of changes to downstream river flows, nutrient ratios, and sediment loads24–26. However, explicit consideration of how seagrass ecosystems may be impacted by dam construction and operation is lacking. Sixty-three percent of the world’s very long rivers are no longer free flowing27, and many of the remaining rivers are planned for impoundment28. Most studies on the ecological impacts of hydroelectric development focus on river and reservoir systems25–27, while impacts on coastal ecosystems remain unclear.

Here, we present a synthesis of recent evidence and transdisciplinary knowledge29 to reveal how a social-ecological system connecting eelgrass (Zostera marina, shikaapaashkw), geese (Branta spp., niskandiyiwaapuwaau), and Cree (Eeyou) in subarctic eastern James Bay, Canada (Eeyou Istchee) has been compromised by the effects of local hydroelectric development compounded by climate change. The evidence presented includes diverse forms of knowledge including Eeyou Indigenous Knowledge shared in interviews, long-term eelgrass monitoring data collected over 30 years, and recent research conducted in the region by the authors.

We apply a detection and attribution process30, increasingly emphasized in global change assessments31, to synthesize evidence and infer the causes of the eelgrass social-ecological system collapse in Eeyou Istchee (Fig. 1). This approach, centered on a causal model linking eelgrass health to environmental drivers, pressures, and biological feedbacks (Fig. 2), integrates scientific records, recent fieldwork, and Eeyou knowledge. To reflect the strength of inference and uncertainty, we use terms such as likely, very likely, and may have caused, depending on the weight of evidence. We present this case because large-scale ecological collapses—often linked to past development—are widespread, yet traditional scientific methods alone have struggled to explain or guide responses to them32. This study provides an example showing that attribution can be done even after significant time has passed and with limited quantitative data, especially when supported by partnerships between scientists and local knowledge holders.

---

## Results

Components and collapse of an eelgrass-goose-Eeyou system
In northeast James Bay, a coastal marine social-ecological system was centered around eelgrass and the harvest of geese in the eelgrass habitat prior to and during the 1970s, when waterfowl was a vital source of food for north coast Eeyou, as it had been for time immemorial5,33,34. Tens of thousands of migrating Canada Geese (Branta canadensis) and Atlantic Brant (Branta bernicla horta) visited the eelgrass meadows each fall35. At the time, eastern James Bay supported the largest expanse of eelgrass Zostera marina meadows in North America36. Harvest surveys conducted in the 1970’s documented the annual harvest of more than 50,000 Canada Geese and 6000 Brant by Eeyou hunters living in the coastal communities37.

This eelgrass ecosystem collapsed in the late 1990s5,33,38,39. The collapse was rapidly observed and reported by land users from coastal traplines (i.e., land areas stewarded by a family, where they hold hunting and trapping rights) and by Cree First Nations of Eeyou Istchee. Coinciding with the eelgrass collapse, Eeyou observed a major reduction in the migratory visits of geese during fall, and a corresponding decline in hunting success33. The Eeyou formally reported the changes to Canadian Parliament in 2008, and the change was acknowledged by Fisheries and Oceans Canada32, but no scientific study of the change was initiated by government, academic or industry researchers for a 20-year period.

Coastal Eeyou in Chisasibi (formerly Fort George) associated the loss of eelgrass with hydroelectric development of the La Grande River (LGR)5,39,40. Environmental monitoring reports prepared for Hydro-Québec (the Crown corporation that owns and operates the hydroelectric complex) stated that the decline was most likely linked to natural causes such as wasting disease, climate change, and isostatic rebound33,38. Nevertheless, Eeyou continued to push for an investigation5,39. In 2017, a formal collaboration began between the Eeyou and a team of university-based researchers with a mandate to i) consider Indigenous and scientific knowledge as distinct but equal sources of information29 and ii) seek to identify what caused the eelgrass decline, including the role (if any) of putative drivers, including La Grande Complex hydroelectric power development (Fig. 1, inset).

Presently, with eelgrass meadows still sparse and discontinuous along the coast15, and coastal waters frequently murky15, the fall goose distribution is not predictable41,42. The Eeyou note a social-ecological regime shift marked by increasingly disordered and less productive hunts, leading to the erosion of traditional knowledge43.

Detection of eelgrass change
During the past 40 years, eelgrass underwent a massive decline along the east James Bay coast and failed to fully recover. Eeyou remember eelgrass as consistently widespread and abundant along the north coast of James Bay before the late 1990s5,39,40,44 (Fig. S1). During the 1980s, the Chisasibi First Nation coastal community noted localized eelgrass declines in some traplines near the LGR, but no changes were observed in other coastal communities located away from the influence of the LGR plume. Scientific observations in the 1970s44 and 199136 found eelgrass to be present between depths of 0.5 and 4.0 m, with shoots up to 2.5 m long, biomass in places >1000 g dw m−2, and an estimated areal coverage of ~250 km2. Eelgrass monitoring at six sites near LGR after 1981 noted localized eelgrass losses but no site-wide changes until 1999, when biomass measured at six monitoring sites decreased by about 90% (Fig. 3). Chisasibi Eeyou noted that eelgrass had ceased to be seen frozen in the ice or as beach wrack and deep eelgrass beds had disappeared completely. A survey of eelgrass cover across 87 sites distributed all along the coast, including areas not influenced by the LGR plume33,38, indicated an 88% decrease in the ‘dense’ eelgrass cover class (>50%) between 1996 and 1999 (Fig. 3, inset)15. During 2017–2021, shoot density and cover were still substantially lower than in the 1970s–early 1990s, with no shoots longer than 1.0 m and cover generally sparse or discontinuous (Fig. S2)15,45. Beds were generally patchy and limited to shallow areas (<2 m) (Fig. S3).

Detection of environmental changes
Development of the “La Grande Complex” over three phases increased winter river flows ten-fold causing an enlarged freshwater plume and first increasing then decreasing sediment fluxes to the coastal habitat43,46,47. The complex consists of 11 power generating stations, 74 generating units, and nine reservoirs. During Phase I (1973–1985), four rivers, including the Eastmain River, were partially diverted into the La Grande River (LGR) watershed, increasing its flow. Peak LGR discharge shifted from spring to winter, with February flow rising from 520 m³ s−1 in 1975 to 1750 m³ s−1 in 1980, and 3000 m³ s-1 in 198446. Annual discharge from the Eastmain River after diversion dropped to about 10% of historical values. In Phase II (1987–1996), additional reservoirs and generation stations were added to the La Grande Complex, including La Grande-1 (LG1), <40 km from the bay, with a design flow of 5950 m3 s−143. In Phase III (2002–2013), partial diversion of the Rupert River further increased the average annual LGR discharge to 3782 m3 s−1, about double its pre-development discharge and nearly half the total discharge to James Bay48 (Fig. 4; Tables S1 and S2). In recent years, high winter discharges were sustained at ~4800 m3 s−1 continuously throughout the January–March period47.

Eeyou from coastal traplines near Chisasibi witnessed several environmental changes associated with LGR development including coastal freshening, riverbank erosion, and sediment release into the bay, the latter linked to murkier water and seabed hardening in the eelgrass habitat45. According to oceanographic studies, the ten-fold increase in winter LGR discharge also increased by ten-fold the size of the under-ice freshwater plume along the coast, as indicated by a salinity of 5 in Fig. 1. This increase in the freshwater plume from ~120 km2 to ~1200 km2 extended it into eelgrass habitat 30–40 km north and south of the river mouth46,47. The area of noticeable freshening of surface waters from winter LGR discharge, referred to as the LGR sector, stretched north to Hudson Bay (near Cape Jones)46,47. The winter LGR export of nitrate, the limiting nutrient in the bay’s oligotrophic marine waters, increased more than 10-fold, at the expense of nitrate delivery during spring and summer48,49. Reservoir flooding led to increased downstream fluxes of dissolved and particulate organic matter48,50,51 and, together with riverbank erosion, caused a four-fold increase in annual sediment exports from LGR during 1979–1991, including annual releases of ~1,000,000 t y−1 fine silt and clay50.

Discharge from the Eastmain River after diversion dropped to about 10%, which weakened its influence along the coast. The diversion limited the Eastmain watershed to the coastal plain near the bay dominated by marine clays, silts, and peat bogs. Suspended particulate matter (SPM), colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM), and nutrients increased in Eastmain River water but because of reduced flow, the overall influence of the river decreased43. The Eastmain estuary experienced higher surface salinity, weaker stratification, and altered circulation after the diversion51.

The marine climate in northeast James Bay changed abruptly in the late 1990s. Coastal Eeyou have remarked on the way climate change is transforming coastal ecosystems and mention, in particular, loss of sea ice45. Climate scientists detect a transition in the mid-1990s after 1996 from a relatively stable regime of seasonal ice and surface-water temperature extremes in the broader Hudson Bay region to much greater fluctuations from year to year52. In northeast James Bay, due in part to a strong El Niño, the winter of 1997/1998 was exceptionally warm with low snow cover. Warm air temperatures continued into spring and the regional sea ice broke up in mid-May of 1998 about one month earlier than the mean breakup date during 1982–1997 (Fig. 4B). With ice clearing from northeast James Bay in late May, a spring storm (Figure S4) produced a sediment-rich LGR freshwater plume that was transported northward (Figure S5). Rapid warming of ice-free surface waters led to unseasonably high sea surface temperatures (SSTs) throughout June-October 1998 (Fig. 4C). In total, five high-SST events lasting a total of 79 days occurred during that period that meet the definition of a marine heat wave (MHW; SST exceeding 90th percentile of the baseline for five consecutive days or more (Fig. 4D))53. Prior to the five 1998 MHWs, there were only two MHWs in Eeyou Istchee coastal waters for the entire 1982–1997 period.

Although an exceptional year individually, 1998 is even more notable as a change-point year, meaning that the northeast James Bay system has not returned to pre-1998 conditions in the subsequent 25+ years. Using a Pettitt change-point test, 1998 is a clear change point for sea ice breakup, MHW frequency, and May-July 10-m wind speeds. For June-October SSTs, 1996 is the stronger change-point year; like the other three parameters, there is no significant trend before or after the change point. Thus, since the late 1990s, James Bay has experienced windier springs, earlier sea ice breakup, and hotter, longer, and more frequent MHWs53. Furthermore, what used to be extreme is now the norm: for example, in the warmest year prior to 1996 (1984), the median June–October SST in northeast James Bay was only 4.2°C, whereas an average year now (post-1996) has a median June-October SST of 5.4°C (Fig. 4C). Notably, climate change is not the primary driver for change in river discharge in northeast James Bay. LGR development resulted in a change-point year of 1985 for discharge. Significantly higher discharge since 1998 (130 km3 y−1) compared to 1951–1985 and 1986–1997 (Fig. 4A) may be a function of regulation combined with (inter)decadal variability within the climate system.

Water clarity decreased along the Eeyou Istchee coast both at local and regional scales during recent decades. Eeyou report that coastal marine water changed from transparent blue to murky brown in Chisasibi between 1986 and the early 1990s and a decade later in Wemindji45. Eeyou from both these communities historically could see the bottom (seabed) at depths of 6 m or more, while the southernmost coast around Eastmain and Waskaganish was traditionally marked by colored and turbid water. During 2017–2021, Secchi disc depths along the coast were typically 2 m or less (Fig. S6) and photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) at the seabed (2–4 m) was very low due to light attenuation by a combination of turbidity and CDOM. Four factors are suspected of contributing at various scales to the decreased water clarity in Eeyou Istchee (Fig. 5):

Browning of James Bay waters likely has occurred, based on satellite images that show an increase in absorption by CDOM (a g(440 nm)), between 1998 and 2021 throughout eastern James Bay surface waters, particularly during the month of June after 2010 (Fig. S7). Thus, the increase in CDOM on a coast-wide scale likely explains in part the increased murkiness witnessed by Eeyou in all Eeyou coastal communities over the past 20 years45. The observed coastal browning is likely related to a general increase in river discharge into the bay since the late-1980s54 and rising concentrations of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and CDOM in river water, coherent with regional trends of increasing DOC and CDOM over the past three decades that have been reported for inland waters across northern Canadian landscapes55. Earlier sea ice melt and retreat may also play a role.

Excess sediment and organic matter released from LGR during the four phases of development likely dispersed with the river plume and deposited at and beyond the plume fringes, where current velocities decrease and salinity increases, while another part may have been trapped in eelgrass beds. Both Eeyou and monitoring teams got the impression of increased turbidity along the coastline in 1985, compared to previous years when the water was clearly transparent, even in windy weather. Sediment core data obtained in the LGR sector show high inventories of a watershed soil erosion tracer, 137Cs56, and buried organic matter that could represent a source of nutrients for algal mats (e.g., Cladophora sericea and a host of epiphytic microalgae) that seem to have become more abundant in the shallow bays. Presently, the LGR as it emerges from the last reservoir LG1 is characterized by lower concentrations of nutrients, DOC, and SPM, and lower fluxes of these constituents during the growing season compared to before development; this is due mostly to the retention of particulates within the upstream reservoirs and the shifting of discharge into winter48,49. However, there is an additional, unquantified but potentially significant SPM flux due to bank erosion in the lowest reach of the river43,57 that could result in events of high riverine delivery of suspended materials, likely at times of peak river discharge during winter. Nutrient release from sediments due to degradation of previously buried organic matter has not been quantified.

Sediment destabilized after loss of eelgrass meadows, exacerbated by more extreme weather and longer open-water season, likely is being recycled in the nearshore area, contributing to a coastal turbid fringe. Eeyou use the word “aayoshtinuukticj” to describe how large eelgrass meadows with long shoots that reached the surface at low tide historically calmed the waters in the bays5. With today’s shorter shoots and lower shoot density (Fig. 3) comes a decrease in the calming effect. Sediment core geochemical profiles show that previously stored sediment was destabilized and eroded after loss of the eelgrass meadows, releasing carbon, nitrogen, and other elements; furthermore, surviving eelgrass beds are not trapping much sediment on an ongoing basis, leading to increased water turbidity23,58. Sediment nutrients that go unused by eelgrass may stimulate increased presence of algal mats, as seen in Danish coastal waters59. Wave-driven sediment resuspension may be exacerbated by increased spring wind velocities and the lengthening of the ice-free season. High-resolution satellite imagery shows that turbid waters with SPM concentrations up to 30 mg L−1 can be pervasive in the nearshore waters along the coastline (Fig. S8).

Attribution of changes in eelgrass to changes in drivers
We use the causal model (Fig. 2) to synthesize evidence for strong relationships between changes in eelgrass health and environmental conditions. We structure the analysis around four time periods related to the eelgrass crash, recognizing the evolution of the role of the Eelgrass-sediment-light (ESL) feedback as eelgrass declined. We do not attribute any large-scale changes in eelgrass to the Eastmain diversion because of the small spatial scale of the known environmental effects (Fig. 5).

Low salinity (<5), which adversely affects the ability of eelgrass to maintain a positive carbon balance (i.e., net primary production)60,61, likely started affecting eelgrass growth in the LGR sector when the winter plume enlarged in the 1980s. Negative effects on carbon balance may particularly jeopardize eelgrasses in high-latitude environments, which require substantial carbohydrate reserves to survive long light-limited winters62,63. The tolerance of eelgrass to low salinity varies across populations but salinity ≤5 consistently reduces eelgrass productivity and survival60,61. Thus, it is very likely that expansion of the LGR winter plume from ~120 km2 to ~1200 km2 reduced eelgrass winter survival and early spring growth in the affected area.

Reduced water clarity during the growing season likely started affecting eelgrass growth in the LGR sector when reservoir flooding and bank collapse increased sediment and organic matter releases in the 1980s. High sediment and organic matter loads can directly reduce water clarity or indirectly (via the ESL feedback) reduce water clarity by smothering eelgrass shoots or causing problems associated with decaying organic matter that impact eelgrass growth. Eelgrass needs clear waters for growth because it has a higher light requirement than both macroalgae and phytoplankton, with an average minimum light requirement of ~20–30% of surface irradiance60. We suspect that light started to decrease in parts of the LGR sector when hydroelectrical development started, due to a combination of excess sediment and organic matter releases from LGR and reduced flocculation from the additional freshwater. Local eelgrass losses would have released previously stored sediments and nitrogen64, likely exacerbating the poor water clarity and starting to shift the eelgrass ecosystem toward a regime shift (Fig. 6E).

Eelgrass growth all along the coast was likely affected by the climate shift and extreme events starting in 1998. The early ice breakup, unseasonably high SSTs and prolonged MHWs in the early part of the 1998 growing season (May, June, and July) may have caused eelgrass to experience extreme negative carbon balance leading to poor growth and/or high mortality. Experimental studies have shown that unusually warm winter-to-spring conditions when light is still limited can have severe effects on eelgrass by accelerating the consumption of energy reserves, which are low following winter, and by triggering early spring flowering65.

Eelgrass recovery likely has been limited by suboptimal water column light levels, partly due to browning and partly from turbidity, combined with a new, more variable, climate regime. An experiment that determined ex situ production-irradiance curves for eelgrass from two Eeyou meadows and collected in situ light data during summer 2021 (continuous measurements of PAR) found suboptimal light conditions for eelgrass growth66. The growing season in James Bay is short, and eelgrass plants need to build up substantial carbon stores during that period to survive the long under-ice period. Because suboptimal water column light levels threaten the ability of eelgrass to build up these stores, we suspect that light limitation has limited eelgrass recovery in the region.

## Methods

Statistics and reproducibility
This study was co-designed with Indigenous Cree (Eeyou) First Nation partners through processes developed under research agreements with Niskamoon and the project steering committee29. Eeyou land users conducted fieldwork along the coast between January 2016 and August 2021 and participated in several iterations of data analysis, interpretation, and review. Details on the interweaving of Eeyou knowledge and science through informal channels are given in Fink-Mercier et al.29 and the project’s final report82, which is published online at https://doi.org/10.34992/4K4Z-TF96. Through formal interviews, Eeyou participated in recording their knowledge between July 2019 and June 2022 including 27 coastal traplines and 66 semi-structured and participatory mapping interviews. The study engaged 95 Eeyou land users, including tallymen and elders. Thus, Indigenous knowledge was central to this study, influencing planning, data collection, analysis, synthesis, result presentations, and final reports, alongside Western science.

Statistical analyses of scientific data were conducted in accordance with standards in each field. For eelgrass shoot density, sample size reflected availability of past monitoring data (1982 to 2009). Using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs; R-package gamm4), we tested for temporal trends in eelgrass shoot density assuming a negative binomial error distribution. No data were excluded from the analyses15. The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. For analysis of environmental times series, a Pettitt test (a non-parametric test for change points) and two-tailed Mann–Whitney test (assessing difference in medians) around the best change point year of 1998 were applied. The null hypothesis was no step change (p<0.05 comparing before/after 1998 for all variables). Experiments were used to test the nutrient and light limitation hypotheses. In the former, we experimentally manipulated plot-level water column nutrient concentration in situ at two sites and compared eelgrass growth in manipulated and control quadrats66. At each site, we set up 3 parallel transects at least 5 m from the edge of the meadow using SCUBA and randomly assigned experimental treatments to 25×25 cm quadrats every 5 m along each transect. To assess the ability of eelgrass to grow under low light conditions, we used 8 whole, randomly selected shoots collected from within the experimental array at each site to construct production–irradiance (PI) curves66.

Ethics and inclusion statement
The knowledge of the Eeyou is well suited to detecting change as their harvesting activities rely on observations of their environment at multiple scales40,42,45. The Indigenous knowledge component of this study was community-driven, with input from Eeyou land users, eelgrass ecologists, waterfowl experts, and the project’s steering committee29. Eeyou engagement in every step of the research was specified in the formal research agreements between the Eeyou organizations and the universities, and these terms were adhered to by the university researchers. These agreements specified protocols for returning all data to the communities and respecting privacy of material in interviews, consistent with established FAIR and CARE principles. The Behavioral Research Ethics Board of the University of British Columbia approved the components of this research that relied on formal interviews with Eeyou people (H20-02942)45. This work fully complies with the Tri-Council Policy Statement: Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans (TCPS 2 2018). The ethical obligations surrounding informed consent in research involving Indigenous Peoples align with Article 9.1 of the TCPS. Additionally, this study adhered to the principles outlined in individual Research and Information Sharing Agreements executed between the principal investigator and the respective First Nations Governments.

Eelgrass abundance, nutrient content and depth delineation
To compile information on eelgrass biomass and density in Eeyou Istchee, Hydro-Québec monitoring reports were reviewed and all raw observations were compiled15. Eelgrass biomass monitoring was a main method of monitoring. Six eelgrass beds within the LGR sector were monitored for shoot density and biomass by Hydro-Québec between 1982 and 2009 to assess the impacts of La Grande development. Eelgrass biomass was assessed at a larger number of locations along the coast in 2019. Eelgrass cover monitoring was the second method employed between 1999 and 201915. Cover classes were assigned according to four abundance classes (Fig. S2).

To assess eelgrass beds depth range, we conducted side-scan sonar surveys using an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) at seven coastal locations in 2019. The AUV was equipped with a Klein side-scan sonar, a conductivity and temperature sensor, and a 10-beam Doppler velocity logger (DVL) for underwater navigation and AUV to the seafloor distance measurement81. A square grid of 20×20 m was overlaid on the side-scan sonar imagery and each grid cell classified by eye as one of: bare seabed, patchy eelgrass, or continuous eelgrass. Water depths along the survey lines were retrieved and sorted into depth bins for each of the classified areas to produce histograms of the water depth distribution of the eelgrass.

To assess energy reserves and nutrient limitation, we measured eelgrass C content in the roots and N in leaves in 2019, respectively. To assess contribution of water column and sediment nutrient sources, we also analyzed the N isotopic ratio (δ15N) in eelgrass shoots83.

To test if light and nutrient levels in the water limit eelgrass growth, we conducted experiments on eelgrass from two beds south of Chisasibi. For nutrient limitation, we manipulated water column nutrient concentrations and compared eelgrass growth in high-nutrient (manipulated) and ambient-nutrient (controlled) conditions at each site66. SCUBA divers measured eelgrass growth rates using a standard protocol. For light limitation, we collected shoots from each eelgrass bed, brought them to a field laboratory, and manipulated light levels. Evidence of light limitation was obtained by comparing eelgrass light requirements with light records from sampling sites.

Remote sensing of ice breakup and sea surface temperature
To compare with eelgrass metrics, time series of environmental variables were compiled and examined15. Mean daily sea surface temperatures of June (°C) for James Bay were obtained from the Group for High Resolution Sea Surface Temperature (GHRSST) product ‘AVHRR_OI-NCEI-L4-GLOB-v2.1’, which provides continuous daily record of SST on a 0.25° spatial grid from 1982 to 2019. The regional annual ice breakup dates were determined from regional ice charts produced by the Canadian Ice Service. Regional sea-level pressure and wind fields at hourly temporal resolution and 0.25° spatial resolution were acquired from the fifth-generation reanalysis (ERA5) of the European Center of Medium-Range Weather Forecasts84,85. Annual freshwater discharge was estimated for the large watershed sectors of the JB from 1951 to 202186. Marine heat wave (MHW) frequency, duration, and intensity for 1982 to 2021 for eastern James Bay were described using the SST dataset from the Operational Sea Surface Temperature and Sea Ice Analysis (OSTIA) system53. This system generates high-resolution (1/20° grid), daily, global, gap-filled SST fields derived from satellite and in situ data. MHW events were defined by five days of sustained warming above the 90th percentile for a 40-year baseline period (1982-2021) for at least five consecutive days87.

Ocean color remote sensing
Concentrations of optically active biogeochemical compounds, i.e., colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and suspended particulate matter (SPM) in the bay were assessed through satellite remote sensing. Regionally tuned empirical algorithms were used to compute CDOM absorbance (a g(400 nm)) and SPM concentrations based on in situ reflectance, CDOM, and SPM data collected in 2018 and 2019 within the scope of the CHCRP88. For the analysis of long-term changes to CDOM, data from the Moderate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer onboard the Aqua satellite (MODIS-Aqua) were atmospherically corrected using a modified version of SeaDAS v889. For the estimation of SPM concentrations, data from the Multi Spectral Imager (MSI) onboard Sentinel-2 (atmospherically corrected using ACOLITE90) was used. Log-transformed values for satellite derived SPM concentrations were mapped to evaluate the spatial variability along the coast as observed by Sentinel-2A MSI on August 8, 2016.

In situ water parameters
To compare the extent of the La Grande River plume to pre-development extent, we carried out a detailed study of the plume when the LGR discharge averaged 4800 m3 s−1 in the winters of 2016 and 201747. Salinity was measured using a conductivity-temperature-depth probe (CTD) and recorded continuously from January to April using ice-deployed moorings. Additionally, discrete CTD profiles were taken all along the coast in all four seasons from 2017 to 2021, and water samples were collected and analyzed for salinity49,91.

To assess the seasonal availability of nutrients in coastal surface waters, nitrate and phosphate were measured in water samples from the LGR sector during early winter, late winter, and summer (2016 and 2017)49, and from sites distributed all along the eastern coast of James Bay during winter (2018, 2019 and 2020), spring (2018 and 2019), summer (2018, 2019 and 2021), and fall (2017 and 2018)91. Sampling stations were located within 25 km of the shore.

Sediment cores
To assess whether erosion had occurred, sediment cores up to 58 cm in length were collected across six Chisasibi traplines between 2017 and 2021 using a gravity corer and push corer as described previously56. The sediment cores were sectioned immediately and subsections analyzed to obtain profiles of the natural radioisotope 210Pb and the artificial radionuclide 137Cs, which is expected to be present in coastal sediments continuously deposited since ca. 195456.

We disagree with the Reviewer here; although perhaps the issue is one of scale. According to references cited in the text and other references we reviewed, the trajectory of seagrass recovery after a decline depends on the intensity of stressors over space and time, the seagrass species, and the location (length of growing season). Full recovery after large-scale declines of perennial seagrass species like eelgrass often takes decades (O’Brien et al. 2018 – ref 72 in the manuscript) — and in some cases, recovery may never occur, even after stressors are removed (Moksnes et al. 2018 – ref 77 in the manuscript). Vaudrey et al. (2010) give some other examples of partial seagrass recoveries after losses. For example, they note that Mumford Cove exhibited a 3–5 year time lag between nutrient load reduction and the initiation of seagrass recolonization and a 12–15 year time lag to a relatively stable distribution. In other cases of recovery, the time to initial establishment for sites with no pre-existing seagrass beds ranged from 3 to 8 y (St. Martin River, Boston Harbor) and expansion of seagrass into stable beds ranged from 7 to 16 y. Maximum cover was achieved in 14 to 22 y (Chincoteague, Sarasota, and Tampa bays). Another important point is that what eelgrass ecosystem “recovery” means to Indigenous rights holders and harvesters vs. outside researchers or agencies is quite different. In the case of James Bay, the Eeyou consider ecosystem recovery to include the deep eelgrass and the massive shallow meadows that historically attracted large numbers of geese.
In direct response to the reviewer’s point about wasting disease, the only study with clear data on pre-wasting disease eelgrass extent demonstrates that full recovery never occurred (Krause-Jensen et al. 2021 – ref 16 in the manuscript).

You are a senior editor at Nature Communications.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

Respond with EXACTLY one of these labels on the first line:

## Paper

## Abstract

Global declines in coastal habitats and wildlife have devastating consequences for Indigenous Peoples. In some places, hydropower development has environmental impacts that contribute significantly to coastal habitat loss. As development is rejuvenated for the carbon-neutral transition, mitigation of further coastal habitat impacts depends on assessing the relative and interactive effects of climate change and hydropower development. Here, we follow a detection and attribution framework to understand the collapse and limited recovery of a social-ecological system including eelgrass (Zostera marina, shikaapaashkw), geese (Branta spp., niskandiyiwaapuwaau), and Cree (Eeyou) in subarctic eastern James Bay, Canada (Eeyou Istchee). Informed by historical observations, Indigenous knowledge, and scientific research, we attribute the collapse of eelgrass and shifts in the associated social-ecological system to ecological effects of hydroelectric development (1978-1996), which degraded local environments causing eelgrass declines. Climate-driven extreme events (1998 onward) compounded losses and ecological feedbacks extended eelgrass declines all along the coast. Eelgrass recovery today appears limited by poor water clarity, altered sediments, hydrologic changes from development, and a new climate regime. Eeyou have adapted by shifting their relationships with the coastal habitat. Comprehensive assessments for hydropower developments should explicitly consider coastal social-ecological dynamics and the possible compounding impacts of climate change.

---

## Introduction

Coastal habitats have supported human communities for hundreds of thousands of years. Coastlines provide food, shelter, and access to marine and freshwater environments that define the culture, livelihoods, and identities of Indigenous Peoples who have lived along marine shorelines for countless generations1. The destruction and loss of coastal habitats worldwide during the past century2 thus has gravely affected both social systems and ecosystems3. Coastal habitat protection, management and restoration can contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation4,5, biodiversity conservation6, and Indigenous self-determination. However, the interaction of local and global environmental change to cause habitat loss and prevent habitat recovery4 is a critical knowledge gap compromising current coastal restoration efforts and preventing true cost accounting of various development activities.

Seagrasses are foundation species in many coastal ecosystems. They provide critical habitat for marine and semi-aquatic wildlife, such as waterfowl, and the reliable, nearshore wildlife harvesting opportunities in seagrass ecosystems have been particularly important for many coastal Indigenous Peoples’ food security and cultural continuity (cf. 5–9). Recently, seagrass ecosystems have also gained attention because of their tendency to accumulate carbon (“blue carbon”), in addition to being biodiversity hotspots. Protecting and restoring degraded seagrass ecosystems may thus contribute to numerous benefits for both Indigenous and non-Indigenous coastal communities, as well as for the ecosystems themselves10–12.

Many seagrass populations around the globe have massively declined in the past century. Few have fully recovered to their historical depth and spatial extents, although North Atlantic eelgrass lost to widespread wasting disease in the 1930s is considered naturally recovered in many areas, and recovered as a result of active restoration in other areas13,14. Incomplete recovery of degraded seagrass ecosystems is often characterized by lower shoot density15, reduced depth extent16, and/or reduced spatial extent16–18 of meadows relative to historical observations, as well as reduced usage by wildlife and ecological functions such as carbon storage19. The reasons for failure to fully recover can be unclear, especially when proximate causes of declines and related environmental conditions have improved18–21.

Among the potential ultimate causes of ecological changes in seagrass ecosystems are local and regional land use and development activities in watersheds that alter riverine fluxes of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment, and cause localized deterioration of water quality and poor water column light conditions due to elevated concentrations of suspended sediments13,14. Sedimentation is a well-recognized stressor because it can disrupt the natural feedback loops that keep seagrass meadows healthy: i.e., excess sediment makes water more turbid, reducing light availability and consequently slowing seagrass growth22,23. Dams are well-know drivers of changes to downstream river flows, nutrient ratios, and sediment loads24–26. However, explicit consideration of how seagrass ecosystems may be impacted by dam construction and operation is lacking. Sixty-three percent of the world’s very long rivers are no longer free flowing27, and many of the remaining rivers are planned for impoundment28. Most studies on the ecological impacts of hydroelectric development focus on river and reservoir systems25–27, while impacts on coastal ecosystems remain unclear.

Here, we present a synthesis of recent evidence and transdisciplinary knowledge29 to reveal how a social-ecological system connecting eelgrass (Zostera marina, shikaapaashkw), geese (Branta spp., niskandiyiwaapuwaau), and Cree (Eeyou) in subarctic eastern James Bay, Canada (Eeyou Istchee) has been compromised by the effects of local hydroelectric development compounded by climate change. The evidence presented includes diverse forms of knowledge including Eeyou Indigenous Knowledge shared in interviews, long-term eelgrass monitoring data collected over 30 years, and recent research conducted in the region by the authors.

We apply a detection and attribution process30, increasingly emphasized in global change assessments31, to synthesize evidence and infer the causes of the eelgrass social-ecological system collapse in Eeyou Istchee (Fig. 1). This approach, centered on a causal model linking eelgrass health to environmental drivers, pressures, and biological feedbacks (Fig. 2), integrates scientific records, recent fieldwork, and Eeyou knowledge. To reflect the strength of inference and uncertainty, we use terms such as likely, very likely, and may have caused, depending on the weight of evidence. We present this case because large-scale ecological collapses—often linked to past development—are widespread, yet traditional scientific methods alone have struggled to explain or guide responses to them32. This study provides an example showing that attribution can be done even after significant time has passed and with limited quantitative data, especially when supported by partnerships between scientists and local knowledge holders.

---

## Results

Components and collapse of an eelgrass-goose-Eeyou system
In northeast James Bay, a coastal marine social-ecological system was centered around eelgrass and the harvest of geese in the eelgrass habitat prior to and during the 1970s, when waterfowl was a vital source of food for north coast Eeyou, as it had been for time immemorial5,33,34. Tens of thousands of migrating Canada Geese (Branta canadensis) and Atlantic Brant (Branta bernicla horta) visited the eelgrass meadows each fall35. At the time, eastern James Bay supported the largest expanse of eelgrass Zostera marina meadows in North America36. Harvest surveys conducted in the 1970’s documented the annual harvest of more than 50,000 Canada Geese and 6000 Brant by Eeyou hunters living in the coastal communities37.

This eelgrass ecosystem collapsed in the late 1990s5,33,38,39. The collapse was rapidly observed and reported by land users from coastal traplines (i.e., land areas stewarded by a family, where they hold hunting and trapping rights) and by Cree First Nations of Eeyou Istchee. Coinciding with the eelgrass collapse, Eeyou observed a major reduction in the migratory visits of geese during fall, and a corresponding decline in hunting success33. The Eeyou formally reported the changes to Canadian Parliament in 2008, and the change was acknowledged by Fisheries and Oceans Canada32, but no scientific study of the change was initiated by government, academic or industry researchers for a 20-year period.

Coastal Eeyou in Chisasibi (formerly Fort George) associated the loss of eelgrass with hydroelectric development of the La Grande River (LGR)5,39,40. Environmental monitoring reports prepared for Hydro-Québec (the Crown corporation that owns and operates the hydroelectric complex) stated that the decline was most likely linked to natural causes such as wasting disease, climate change, and isostatic rebound33,38. Nevertheless, Eeyou continued to push for an investigation5,39. In 2017, a formal collaboration began between the Eeyou and a team of university-based researchers with a mandate to i) consider Indigenous and scientific knowledge as distinct but equal sources of information29 and ii) seek to identify what caused the eelgrass decline, including the role (if any) of putative drivers, including La Grande Complex hydroelectric power development (Fig. 1, inset).

Presently, with eelgrass meadows still sparse and discontinuous along the coast15, and coastal waters frequently murky15, the fall goose distribution is not predictable41,42. The Eeyou note a social-ecological regime shift marked by increasingly disordered and less productive hunts, leading to the erosion of traditional knowledge43.

Detection of eelgrass change
During the past 40 years, eelgrass underwent a massive decline along the east James Bay coast and failed to fully recover. Eeyou remember eelgrass as consistently widespread and abundant along the north coast of James Bay before the late 1990s5,39,40,44 (Fig. S1). During the 1980s, the Chisasibi First Nation coastal community noted localized eelgrass declines in some traplines near the LGR, but no changes were observed in other coastal communities located away from the influence of the LGR plume. Scientific observations in the 1970s44 and 199136 found eelgrass to be present between depths of 0.5 and 4.0 m, with shoots up to 2.5 m long, biomass in places >1000 g dw m−2, and an estimated areal coverage of ~250 km2. Eelgrass monitoring at six sites near LGR after 1981 noted localized eelgrass losses but no site-wide changes until 1999, when biomass measured at six monitoring sites decreased by about 90% (Fig. 3). Chisasibi Eeyou noted that eelgrass had ceased to be seen frozen in the ice or as beach wrack and deep eelgrass beds had disappeared completely. A survey of eelgrass cover across 87 sites distributed all along the coast, including areas not influenced by the LGR plume33,38, indicated an 88% decrease in the ‘dense’ eelgrass cover class (>50%) between 1996 and 1999 (Fig. 3, inset)15. During 2017–2021, shoot density and cover were still substantially lower than in the 1970s–early 1990s, with no shoots longer than 1.0 m and cover generally sparse or discontinuous (Fig. S2)15,45. Beds were generally patchy and limited to shallow areas (<2 m) (Fig. S3).

Detection of environmental changes
Development of the “La Grande Complex” over three phases increased winter river flows ten-fold causing an enlarged freshwater plume and first increasing then decreasing sediment fluxes to the coastal habitat43,46,47. The complex consists of 11 power generating stations, 74 generating units, and nine reservoirs. During Phase I (1973–1985), four rivers, including the Eastmain River, were partially diverted into the La Grande River (LGR) watershed, increasing its flow. Peak LGR discharge shifted from spring to winter, with February flow rising from 520 m³ s−1 in 1975 to 1750 m³ s−1 in 1980, and 3000 m³ s-1 in 198446. Annual discharge from the Eastmain River after diversion dropped to about 10% of historical values. In Phase II (1987–1996), additional reservoirs and generation stations were added to the La Grande Complex, including La Grande-1 (LG1), <40 km from the bay, with a design flow of 5950 m3 s−143. In Phase III (2002–2013), partial diversion of the Rupert River further increased the average annual LGR discharge to 3782 m3 s−1, about double its pre-development discharge and nearly half the total discharge to James Bay48 (Fig. 4; Tables S1 and S2). In recent years, high winter discharges were sustained at ~4800 m3 s−1 continuously throughout the January–March period47.

Eeyou from coastal traplines near Chisasibi witnessed several environmental changes associated with LGR development including coastal freshening, riverbank erosion, and sediment release into the bay, the latter linked to murkier water and seabed hardening in the eelgrass habitat45. According to oceanographic studies, the ten-fold increase in winter LGR discharge also increased by ten-fold the size of the under-ice freshwater plume along the coast, as indicated by a salinity of 5 in Fig. 1. This increase in the freshwater plume from ~120 km2 to ~1200 km2 extended it into eelgrass habitat 30–40 km north and south of the river mouth46,47. The area of noticeable freshening of surface waters from winter LGR discharge, referred to as the LGR sector, stretched north to Hudson Bay (near Cape Jones)46,47. The winter LGR export of nitrate, the limiting nutrient in the bay’s oligotrophic marine waters, increased more than 10-fold, at the expense of nitrate delivery during spring and summer48,49. Reservoir flooding led to increased downstream fluxes of dissolved and particulate organic matter48,50,51 and, together with riverbank erosion, caused a four-fold increase in annual sediment exports from LGR during 1979–1991, including annual releases of ~1,000,000 t y−1 fine silt and clay50.

Discharge from the Eastmain River after diversion dropped to about 10%, which weakened its influence along the coast. The diversion limited the Eastmain watershed to the coastal plain near the bay dominated by marine clays, silts, and peat bogs. Suspended particulate matter (SPM), colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM), and nutrients increased in Eastmain River water but because of reduced flow, the overall influence of the river decreased43. The Eastmain estuary experienced higher surface salinity, weaker stratification, and altered circulation after the diversion51.

The marine climate in northeast James Bay changed abruptly in the late 1990s. Coastal Eeyou have remarked on the way climate change is transforming coastal ecosystems and mention, in particular, loss of sea ice45. Climate scientists detect a transition in the mid-1990s after 1996 from a relatively stable regime of seasonal ice and surface-water temperature extremes in the broader Hudson Bay region to much greater fluctuations from year to year52. In northeast James Bay, due in part to a strong El Niño, the winter of 1997/1998 was exceptionally warm with low snow cover. Warm air temperatures continued into spring and the regional sea ice broke up in mid-May of 1998 about one month earlier than the mean breakup date during 1982–1997 (Fig. 4B). With ice clearing from northeast James Bay in late May, a spring storm (Figure S4) produced a sediment-rich LGR freshwater plume that was transported northward (Figure S5). Rapid warming of ice-free surface waters led to unseasonably high sea surface temperatures (SSTs) throughout June-October 1998 (Fig. 4C). In total, five high-SST events lasting a total of 79 days occurred during that period that meet the definition of a marine heat wave (MHW; SST exceeding 90th percentile of the baseline for five consecutive days or more (Fig. 4D))53. Prior to the five 1998 MHWs, there were only two MHWs in Eeyou Istchee coastal waters for the entire 1982–1997 period.

Although an exceptional year individually, 1998 is even more notable as a change-point year, meaning that the northeast James Bay system has not returned to pre-1998 conditions in the subsequent 25+ years. Using a Pettitt change-point test, 1998 is a clear change point for sea ice breakup, MHW frequency, and May-July 10-m wind speeds. For June-October SSTs, 1996 is the stronger change-point year; like the other three parameters, there is no significant trend before or after the change point. Thus, since the late 1990s, James Bay has experienced windier springs, earlier sea ice breakup, and hotter, longer, and more frequent MHWs53. Furthermore, what used to be extreme is now the norm: for example, in the warmest year prior to 1996 (1984), the median June–October SST in northeast James Bay was only 4.2°C, whereas an average year now (post-1996) has a median June-October SST of 5.4°C (Fig. 4C). Notably, climate change is not the primary driver for change in river discharge in northeast James Bay. LGR development resulted in a change-point year of 1985 for discharge. Significantly higher discharge since 1998 (130 km3 y−1) compared to 1951–1985 and 1986–1997 (Fig. 4A) may be a function of regulation combined with (inter)decadal variability within the climate system.

Water clarity decreased along the Eeyou Istchee coast both at local and regional scales during recent decades. Eeyou report that coastal marine water changed from transparent blue to murky brown in Chisasibi between 1986 and the early 1990s and a decade later in Wemindji45. Eeyou from both these communities historically could see the bottom (seabed) at depths of 6 m or more, while the southernmost coast around Eastmain and Waskaganish was traditionally marked by colored and turbid water. During 2017–2021, Secchi disc depths along the coast were typically 2 m or less (Fig. S6) and photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) at the seabed (2–4 m) was very low due to light attenuation by a combination of turbidity and CDOM. Four factors are suspected of contributing at various scales to the decreased water clarity in Eeyou Istchee (Fig. 5):

Browning of James Bay waters likely has occurred, based on satellite images that show an increase in absorption by CDOM (a g(440 nm)), between 1998 and 2021 throughout eastern James Bay surface waters, particularly during the month of June after 2010 (Fig. S7). Thus, the increase in CDOM on a coast-wide scale likely explains in part the increased murkiness witnessed by Eeyou in all Eeyou coastal communities over the past 20 years45. The observed coastal browning is likely related to a general increase in river discharge into the bay since the late-1980s54 and rising concentrations of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and CDOM in river water, coherent with regional trends of increasing DOC and CDOM over the past three decades that have been reported for inland waters across northern Canadian landscapes55. Earlier sea ice melt and retreat may also play a role.

Excess sediment and organic matter released from LGR during the four phases of development likely dispersed with the river plume and deposited at and beyond the plume fringes, where current velocities decrease and salinity increases, while another part may have been trapped in eelgrass beds. Both Eeyou and monitoring teams got the impression of increased turbidity along the coastline in 1985, compared to previous years when the water was clearly transparent, even in windy weather. Sediment core data obtained in the LGR sector show high inventories of a watershed soil erosion tracer, 137Cs56, and buried organic matter that could represent a source of nutrients for algal mats (e.g., Cladophora sericea and a host of epiphytic microalgae) that seem to have become more abundant in the shallow bays. Presently, the LGR as it emerges from the last reservoir LG1 is characterized by lower concentrations of nutrients, DOC, and SPM, and lower fluxes of these constituents during the growing season compared to before development; this is due mostly to the retention of particulates within the upstream reservoirs and the shifting of discharge into winter48,49. However, there is an additional, unquantified but potentially significant SPM flux due to bank erosion in the lowest reach of the river43,57 that could result in events of high riverine delivery of suspended materials, likely at times of peak river discharge during winter. Nutrient release from sediments due to degradation of previously buried organic matter has not been quantified.

Sediment destabilized after loss of eelgrass meadows, exacerbated by more extreme weather and longer open-water season, likely is being recycled in the nearshore area, contributing to a coastal turbid fringe. Eeyou use the word “aayoshtinuukticj” to describe how large eelgrass meadows with long shoots that reached the surface at low tide historically calmed the waters in the bays5. With today’s shorter shoots and lower shoot density (Fig. 3) comes a decrease in the calming effect. Sediment core geochemical profiles show that previously stored sediment was destabilized and eroded after loss of the eelgrass meadows, releasing carbon, nitrogen, and other elements; furthermore, surviving eelgrass beds are not trapping much sediment on an ongoing basis, leading to increased water turbidity23,58. Sediment nutrients that go unused by eelgrass may stimulate increased presence of algal mats, as seen in Danish coastal waters59. Wave-driven sediment resuspension may be exacerbated by increased spring wind velocities and the lengthening of the ice-free season. High-resolution satellite imagery shows that turbid waters with SPM concentrations up to 30 mg L−1 can be pervasive in the nearshore waters along the coastline (Fig. S8).

Attribution of changes in eelgrass to changes in drivers
We use the causal model (Fig. 2) to synthesize evidence for strong relationships between changes in eelgrass health and environmental conditions. We structure the analysis around four time periods related to the eelgrass crash, recognizing the evolution of the role of the Eelgrass-sediment-light (ESL) feedback as eelgrass declined. We do not attribute any large-scale changes in eelgrass to the Eastmain diversion because of the small spatial scale of the known environmental effects (Fig. 5).

Low salinity (<5), which adversely affects the ability of eelgrass to maintain a positive carbon balance (i.e., net primary production)60,61, likely started affecting eelgrass growth in the LGR sector when the winter plume enlarged in the 1980s. Negative effects on carbon balance may particularly jeopardize eelgrasses in high-latitude environments, which require substantial carbohydrate reserves to survive long light-limited winters62,63. The tolerance of eelgrass to low salinity varies across populations but salinity ≤5 consistently reduces eelgrass productivity and survival60,61. Thus, it is very likely that expansion of the LGR winter plume from ~120 km2 to ~1200 km2 reduced eelgrass winter survival and early spring growth in the affected area.

Reduced water clarity during the growing season likely started affecting eelgrass growth in the LGR sector when reservoir flooding and bank collapse increased sediment and organic matter releases in the 1980s. High sediment and organic matter loads can directly reduce water clarity or indirectly (via the ESL feedback) reduce water clarity by smothering eelgrass shoots or causing problems associated with decaying organic matter that impact eelgrass growth. Eelgrass needs clear waters for growth because it has a higher light requirement than both macroalgae and phytoplankton, with an average minimum light requirement of ~20–30% of surface irradiance60. We suspect that light started to decrease in parts of the LGR sector when hydroelectrical development started, due to a combination of excess sediment and organic matter releases from LGR and reduced flocculation from the additional freshwater. Local eelgrass losses would have released previously stored sediments and nitrogen64, likely exacerbating the poor water clarity and starting to shift the eelgrass ecosystem toward a regime shift (Fig. 6E).

Eelgrass growth all along the coast was likely affected by the climate shift and extreme events starting in 1998. The early ice breakup, unseasonably high SSTs and prolonged MHWs in the early part of the 1998 growing season (May, June, and July) may have caused eelgrass to experience extreme negative carbon balance leading to poor growth and/or high mortality. Experimental studies have shown that unusually warm winter-to-spring conditions when light is still limited can have severe effects on eelgrass by accelerating the consumption of energy reserves, which are low following winter, and by triggering early spring flowering65.

Eelgrass recovery likely has been limited by suboptimal water column light levels, partly due to browning and partly from turbidity, combined with a new, more variable, climate regime. An experiment that determined ex situ production-irradiance curves for eelgrass from two Eeyou meadows and collected in situ light data during summer 2021 (continuous measurements of PAR) found suboptimal light conditions for eelgrass growth66. The growing season in James Bay is short, and eelgrass plants need to build up substantial carbon stores during that period to survive the long under-ice period. Because suboptimal water column light levels threaten the ability of eelgrass to build up these stores, we suspect that light limitation has limited eelgrass recovery in the region.

## Methods

Statistics and reproducibility
This study was co-designed with Indigenous Cree (Eeyou) First Nation partners through processes developed under research agreements with Niskamoon and the project steering committee29. Eeyou land users conducted fieldwork along the coast between January 2016 and August 2021 and participated in several iterations of data analysis, interpretation, and review. Details on the interweaving of Eeyou knowledge and science through informal channels are given in Fink-Mercier et al.29 and the project’s final report82, which is published online at https://doi.org/10.34992/4K4Z-TF96. Through formal interviews, Eeyou participated in recording their knowledge between July 2019 and June 2022 including 27 coastal traplines and 66 semi-structured and participatory mapping interviews. The study engaged 95 Eeyou land users, including tallymen and elders. Thus, Indigenous knowledge was central to this study, influencing planning, data collection, analysis, synthesis, result presentations, and final reports, alongside Western science.

Statistical analyses of scientific data were conducted in accordance with standards in each field. For eelgrass shoot density, sample size reflected availability of past monitoring data (1982 to 2009). Using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs; R-package gamm4), we tested for temporal trends in eelgrass shoot density assuming a negative binomial error distribution. No data were excluded from the analyses15. The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. For analysis of environmental times series, a Pettitt test (a non-parametric test for change points) and two-tailed Mann–Whitney test (assessing difference in medians) around the best change point year of 1998 were applied. The null hypothesis was no step change (p<0.05 comparing before/after 1998 for all variables). Experiments were used to test the nutrient and light limitation hypotheses. In the former, we experimentally manipulated plot-level water column nutrient concentration in situ at two sites and compared eelgrass growth in manipulated and control quadrats66. At each site, we set up 3 parallel transects at least 5 m from the edge of the meadow using SCUBA and randomly assigned experimental treatments to 25×25 cm quadrats every 5 m along each transect. To assess the ability of eelgrass to grow under low light conditions, we used 8 whole, randomly selected shoots collected from within the experimental array at each site to construct production–irradiance (PI) curves66.

Ethics and inclusion statement
The knowledge of the Eeyou is well suited to detecting change as their harvesting activities rely on observations of their environment at multiple scales40,42,45. The Indigenous knowledge component of this study was community-driven, with input from Eeyou land users, eelgrass ecologists, waterfowl experts, and the project’s steering committee29. Eeyou engagement in every step of the research was specified in the formal research agreements between the Eeyou organizations and the universities, and these terms were adhered to by the university researchers. These agreements specified protocols for returning all data to the communities and respecting privacy of material in interviews, consistent with established FAIR and CARE principles. The Behavioral Research Ethics Board of the University of British Columbia approved the components of this research that relied on formal interviews with Eeyou people (H20-02942)45. This work fully complies with the Tri-Council Policy Statement: Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans (TCPS 2 2018). The ethical obligations surrounding informed consent in research involving Indigenous Peoples align with Article 9.1 of the TCPS. Additionally, this study adhered to the principles outlined in individual Research and Information Sharing Agreements executed between the principal investigator and the respective First Nations Governments.

Eelgrass abundance, nutrient content and depth delineation
To compile information on eelgrass biomass and density in Eeyou Istchee, Hydro-Québec monitoring reports were reviewed and all raw observations were compiled15. Eelgrass biomass monitoring was a main method of monitoring. Six eelgrass beds within the LGR sector were monitored for shoot density and biomass by Hydro-Québec between 1982 and 2009 to assess the impacts of La Grande development. Eelgrass biomass was assessed at a larger number of locations along the coast in 2019. Eelgrass cover monitoring was the second method employed between 1999 and 201915. Cover classes were assigned according to four abundance classes (Fig. S2).

To assess eelgrass beds depth range, we conducted side-scan sonar surveys using an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) at seven coastal locations in 2019. The AUV was equipped with a Klein side-scan sonar, a conductivity and temperature sensor, and a 10-beam Doppler velocity logger (DVL) for underwater navigation and AUV to the seafloor distance measurement81. A square grid of 20×20 m was overlaid on the side-scan sonar imagery and each grid cell classified by eye as one of: bare seabed, patchy eelgrass, or continuous eelgrass. Water depths along the survey lines were retrieved and sorted into depth bins for each of the classified areas to produce histograms of the water depth distribution of the eelgrass.

To assess energy reserves and nutrient limitation, we measured eelgrass C content in the roots and N in leaves in 2019, respectively. To assess contribution of water column and sediment nutrient sources, we also analyzed the N isotopic ratio (δ15N) in eelgrass shoots83.

To test if light and nutrient levels in the water limit eelgrass growth, we conducted experiments on eelgrass from two beds south of Chisasibi. For nutrient limitation, we manipulated water column nutrient concentrations and compared eelgrass growth in high-nutrient (manipulated) and ambient-nutrient (controlled) conditions at each site66. SCUBA divers measured eelgrass growth rates using a standard protocol. For light limitation, we collected shoots from each eelgrass bed, brought them to a field laboratory, and manipulated light levels. Evidence of light limitation was obtained by comparing eelgrass light requirements with light records from sampling sites.

Remote sensing of ice breakup and sea surface temperature
To compare with eelgrass metrics, time series of environmental variables were compiled and examined15. Mean daily sea surface temperatures of June (°C) for James Bay were obtained from the Group for High Resolution Sea Surface Temperature (GHRSST) product ‘AVHRR_OI-NCEI-L4-GLOB-v2.1’, which provides continuous daily record of SST on a 0.25° spatial grid from 1982 to 2019. The regional annual ice breakup dates were determined from regional ice charts produced by the Canadian Ice Service. Regional sea-level pressure and wind fields at hourly temporal resolution and 0.25° spatial resolution were acquired from the fifth-generation reanalysis (ERA5) of the European Center of Medium-Range Weather Forecasts84,85. Annual freshwater discharge was estimated for the large watershed sectors of the JB from 1951 to 202186. Marine heat wave (MHW) frequency, duration, and intensity for 1982 to 2021 for eastern James Bay were described using the SST dataset from the Operational Sea Surface Temperature and Sea Ice Analysis (OSTIA) system53. This system generates high-resolution (1/20° grid), daily, global, gap-filled SST fields derived from satellite and in situ data. MHW events were defined by five days of sustained warming above the 90th percentile for a 40-year baseline period (1982-2021) for at least five consecutive days87.

Ocean color remote sensing
Concentrations of optically active biogeochemical compounds, i.e., colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and suspended particulate matter (SPM) in the bay were assessed through satellite remote sensing. Regionally tuned empirical algorithms were used to compute CDOM absorbance (a g(400 nm)) and SPM concentrations based on in situ reflectance, CDOM, and SPM data collected in 2018 and 2019 within the scope of the CHCRP88. For the analysis of long-term changes to CDOM, data from the Moderate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer onboard the Aqua satellite (MODIS-Aqua) were atmospherically corrected using a modified version of SeaDAS v889. For the estimation of SPM concentrations, data from the Multi Spectral Imager (MSI) onboard Sentinel-2 (atmospherically corrected using ACOLITE90) was used. Log-transformed values for satellite derived SPM concentrations were mapped to evaluate the spatial variability along the coast as observed by Sentinel-2A MSI on August 8, 2016.

In situ water parameters
To compare the extent of the La Grande River plume to pre-development extent, we carried out a detailed study of the plume when the LGR discharge averaged 4800 m3 s−1 in the winters of 2016 and 201747. Salinity was measured using a conductivity-temperature-depth probe (CTD) and recorded continuously from January to April using ice-deployed moorings. Additionally, discrete CTD profiles were taken all along the coast in all four seasons from 2017 to 2021, and water samples were collected and analyzed for salinity49,91.

To assess the seasonal availability of nutrients in coastal surface waters, nitrate and phosphate were measured in water samples from the LGR sector during early winter, late winter, and summer (2016 and 2017)49, and from sites distributed all along the eastern coast of James Bay during winter (2018, 2019 and 2020), spring (2018 and 2019), summer (2018, 2019 and 2021), and fall (2017 and 2018)91. Sampling stations were located within 25 km of the shore.

Sediment cores
To assess whether erosion had occurred, sediment cores up to 58 cm in length were collected across six Chisasibi traplines between 2017 and 2021 using a gravity corer and push corer as described previously56. The sediment cores were sectioned immediately and subsections analyzed to obtain profiles of the natural radioisotope 210Pb and the artificial radionuclide 137Cs, which is expected to be present in coastal sediments continuously deposited since ca. 195456.

We disagree with the Reviewer here; although perhaps the issue is one of scale. According to references cited in the text and other references we reviewed, the trajectory of seagrass recovery after a decline depends on the intensity of stressors over space and time, the seagrass species, and the location (length of growing season). Full recovery after large-scale declines of perennial seagrass species like eelgrass often takes decades (O’Brien et al. 2018 – ref 72 in the manuscript) — and in some cases, recovery may never occur, even after stressors are removed (Moksnes et al. 2018 – ref 77 in the manuscript). For example, they note that Mumford Cove exhibited a 3–5 year time lag between nutrient load reduction and the initiation of seagrass recolonization and a 12–15 year time lag to a relatively stable distribution. In other cases of recovery, the time to initial establishment for sites with no pre-existing seagrass beds ranged from 3 to 8 y (St. Martin River, Boston Harbor) and expansion of seagrass into stable beds ranged from 7 to 16 y. We do not agree with the reviewer on this point and cite a paper that proves eelgrass can grow in winter in northern areas (Olesen et al. 2015 – ref 43 in the manuscript). To quote from this paper, “The long leaf lifespan of these northern eelgrass populations indicates that they maintain metabolically active leaves during winter, as has been observed in other subarctic eelgrass populations and in freshwater macrophytes under winter ice cover (McRoy 1969 – ref 62 in the manuscript, Boylen & Sheldon 1976).” We also have observed eelgrass under the sea ice along the Eeyou Istchee coast (Chris Peck and Zou Zou Kuzyk, unpublished) and found evidence of winter growth in rhizomes of eelgrass from perennial beds (Mary O’Connor and Kaleigh Davis, unpublished data). We do agree that most of the carbon fixation occurs in summer, but this does not rule out that physiological stress during winter or early spring could hinder eelgrass growth and recovery.
